Presume
pre-zūm'
v.i. (to venture without warrant; used of Israel going up without the ark, of the prophet who speaks unsent, and of Haman's daring)
Latin praesumere, to take beforehand. To presume is to take what has not been given — a warrant, an office, a permission — and Scripture treats it as a distinct category of sin, separate from weakness.

Biblical Definition

After the spies' report and the sentence of forty years, Israel changed its mind and went to fight: “But they presumed to go up unto the hill top: nevertheless the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and Moses, departed not out of the camp” (Numbers 14:44). The detail is the point — the ark stayed behind, and so did Moses, and the army went anyway. “Then the Amalekites came down, and the Canaanites which dwelt in that hill, and smote them, and discomfited them” (Numbers 14:45). Doing the right thing a day late, without the command, is not obedience. The second use guards the prophetic office: “But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die” (Deuteronomy 18:20), with the test following in verse 22 — if the thing follow not, the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously. The third is Ahasuerus asking after Haman: “Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so?” (Esther 7:5). In every case the sin is acting on an authority that was never granted.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines presume as to venture without positive leave, to form confident opinions without sufficient evidence, and to make confident or arrogant attempts.

expand to see more

PRESUME, v.t. To take or suppose to be true or entitled to belief, without examination or positive proof.

PRESUME, v.i. To venture without positive leave.

2. To form confident or arrogant opinions; with on or upon.

3. To make confident or arrogant attempts.

PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; adventuring without reasonable ground of success.

Key Scripture

Numbers 14:44 — "But they presumed to go up unto the hill top: nevertheless the ark of the covenant of the LORD, and Moses, departed not out of the camp."

Deuteronomy 18:20 — "But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die."

Numbers 14:45 — "Then the Amalekites came down, and the Canaanites which dwelt in that hill, and smote them, and discomfited them, even unto Hormah."

Deuteronomy 18:22 — "When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him."

Modern Corruption

Speaking for God without a warrant carries a death sentence in Deuteronomy and no consequence at all in the modern church.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 18:20 attaches capital punishment to presuming to speak a word in the LORD's name that He has not commanded, and verse 22 supplies a test anyone can apply: if it does not come to pass, the LORD did not say it. The contemporary market in personal prophecy operates in flat defiance of both. Words are delivered in God's name, they fail, and no one is held to anything — the failure is explained by the hearer's faith or by a shifted timetable. The cessationist position of the Reformed churches follows from the closed canon, but even those who expect continuing revelation have no way around the standard Moses set: God attaches His name to nothing that fails.

Numbers 14 addresses the subtler form, and it is the one that catches earnest people. Israel repented of their unbelief and set out to do the very thing God had originally commanded — and were destroyed, because the command had been withdrawn and the ark did not move. Zeal for a good work is not the same as a commission to do it, and Moses said plainly, go not up, for the LORD is not among you. A man may be doing something Scripture generally commends and still be presuming, if he is doing it in a place and hour where God has not sent him. The mark of the difference is usually visible in advance: the ark stayed in the camp.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew aphal, to swell or be presumptuous — Numbers 14:44; zud, to act proudly or presumptuously — Deuteronomy 18:20, 22; male leb, to fill the heart — Esther 7:5.

expand to see more

Hebrew aphal — to swell, to be lifted up; Numbers 14:44, of the presumption to go up.

Hebrew zud — to act proudly, presumptuously; Deuteronomy 18:20, 18:22, and the sin of presumptuous sins in Psalm 19:13.

Hebrew male leb — to fill the heart, hence to dare; Esther 7:5, who durst presume in his heart.

Hebrew Hormah — destruction; Numbers 14:45, the place the presumption ended.

Psalm 19:13 makes it a matter of prayer: keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me.

Usage

"“They presumed to go up… nevertheless the ark… departed not out of the camp”."

"“If the thing follow not… the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously” — a test anyone can apply."

"Doing the right thing a day late, without the command, is not obedience."
